title: Six Hawaii stations had complete water-level records for 14 PTWC events with no NCEI gauge report in 2015-2026
abstract: We test whether an event-specific count of tsunami reports measures instrument availability. We use all 22 Hawaii forecast pairs in a fixed PTWC study and new NOAA CO-OPS water-level queries at six fixed stations. Each of the 132 station-event windows has all 240 expected six-minute values in the 24 hours after earthquake origin. Fourteen events have no Hawaii tide-gauge report in the prior NCEI extract, although all six stations have complete records. Only 31 of 132 windows have a NCEI report within 2 km. At 0.5 and 5 km, the counts are 24 and 32. Six windows have preliminary data; 126 have at least 95% verified, non-inferred values. Thus report absence does not imply instrument-data absence in this Hawaii sample. A count of event reports can mix spatial sampling with event reporting. This limits its use as a measure of operating network size. The finding does not refute exact withholding tests within reported records. It does not test tsunami amplitudes, real-time telemetry or coastal forecast calibration. Hawaii is one dense region and only two events have threat categories of at least 0.3 m. Code, aggregate results, exact response hashes and retrieval paths are included; external source records remain outside the bundle.

display.caption: Continuous water-level availability and tsunami event reports differ at a fixed six-station Hawaii network in 22 event windows.

citations.reason: We reuse its fixed forecast pairs and NCEI snapshot and test the interpretation of record count as instrument availability.
It separates exact record withholding from coastal identification; we add external instrument availability.
It tests spatial selection within reported sites; our audit tests whether unreported sites have continuous water levels.
